text: Everything you've built so far in this course was supervised — every training row came with a label. Now the labels disappear. Clustering asks a different question: given a table of rows and no target column, which rows naturally belong together? Retailers use it to find customer segments, banks to group similar accounts.

Throughout this chapter we use illustrative retail customers with two features — annual spend and visits per month — with three built-in groups, so we know what a good result should look like. Annual spend runs from about 183 to 1,636, while visits per month run from about 0.7 to 11.9 — very different scales.

Clustering algorithms judge similarity by distance, just like k-NN, so a feature in the hundreds would dominate one in single digits — we standardize first. Running StandardScaler then k-means with three clusters: all three clusters hold exactly 100 customers each, and the silhouette score comes out to 0.773.

The silhouette score runs from negative 1 to 1 and measures how much closer each point is to its own cluster than to the next nearest one — higher is better, and values near 0.7 or above suggest well-separated groups. A cluster label is just a number, though — to make it useful, you profile it by grouping the original unscaled data and comparing averages.

Cluster 0 averages $1,190.60 in spend with 3.1 visits, cluster 1 averages $694.60 with 8.9 visits, and cluster 2 averages $297.00 with 2.0 visits. You could name these big spenders who visit rarely, frequent mid-spenders, and occasional low spenders. The numbers themselves are arbitrary and can change between runs — always name clusters by their profile, never by their number.

Plotting it makes the whole idea concrete — the left panel is what you start with, an unlabeled cloud of dots. The right panel is what clustering returns, the same dots colored into three distinct groups.

Three families of algorithms. Centroid-based, like k-means — each cluster summarized by a center point, fast and simple, best for round, similar-sized groups. Hierarchical, or agglomerative — repeatedly merge the closest points or groups into a tree you can cut at any height. Density-based, like DBSCAN — a cluster is a dense region, sparse points get labeled noise with label negative 1. On our data it finds three groups plus exactly one noise point.

Because there are no labels, nothing tells you a clustering is right. You judge it by whether groups are compact and separated, using the silhouette score, and above all whether they're useful and describable to the business. To recap: clustering finds structure without labels, scale first, profile the groups, and remember the algorithm you choose shapes the groups you get. Next up: k-means in detail.
